summary: Summation No. 33 covers non-military Occupation activities in Japan for June 1948 (data mostly for April-May). Politically the month was dominated by the Nishio political-funds scandal, the Diet budget deadlock, and the Illegal Transactions Investigation Committee's probes of donations and hoarded military supplies, along with rifts in the Democratic Party. The 28 June Fukui earthquake devastated Fukui city and threatened textile rehabilitation. Economic sections report postwar peaks in coke, vacuum tubes, watches and silk fabric, a growing coal output, and new trade machinery: Boeki Cho's direct dealing authority, a $60 million raw-cotton credit and a sterling payment agreement. Labor reports union membership (6.55 million), left-right struggle and wage standards. Social sections cover new pharmaceutical and narcotics laws, repatriation, the Diet's rescinding of the Imperial Rescript on Education, and information programs. Historians will find detailed statistics, war crimes trial figures, land reform totals, and party and Diet legislative detail.
highlights: The House of Representatives rejected nonconfidence in Deputy Prime Minister Nishio 209 to 178 on 24 June over 500,000 yen in unreported political funds, which split the Social Democrats and ended in a 30 June budget compromise.
The 28 June Fukui earthquake destroyed about 70 percent of Fukui city, killing 3,195 and injuring 9,858 there, and threatened rayon and textile rehabilitation.

The Diet enacted the National Property Law on 28 June, creating five classes of public property and a classification commission, and both houses reaffirmed the 1890 Imperial Rescript on Education invalid on 18-19 June.

Boeki Cho was authorized 28 May to deal directly with foreign firms; a $60 million raw-cotton credit, a 31 May sterling payment agreement and a 9 June China trade agreement followed, against a four-month deficit of $200,186,092.
The Cabinet approved a Broadcast Bill on 18 June creating an independent Broadcasting Commission and a nonprofit Broadcasting Corporation of Japan.
By 20 June 673 war crimes suspects had been tried, 623 convicted and 95 sentenced to death; 1,136 internees remained at Sugamo.
Unions numbered 31,075 with 6,553,816 members amid sharpening left-right struggle; the government wage base was set at ¥3,700 for price revisions and 3,791 yen in the budget compromise.
Postwar peaks were reached in coke (254,819 tons), watches and clocks (197,039), and silk fabric (10,631,000 square yards); tenants bought 101,498 cho of land in May.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover, title pages and contents for Summation No. 33 (June 1948): four-part outline, a list of 80 charts, maps and graphs, and a topographic map of Japan.

sections.title: Part I: General
sections.summary: Digest of the month: the Nishio funds charge, 209-178 nonconfidence vote and Fukui earthquake; coal and coke output, union membership of 6.55 million; new pharmaceutical laws and the Rescript on Education resolution.

sections.title: Organization Under SCAP
sections.summary: No change occurred in the non-military organization of General Headquarters, SCAP, during June 1948.

sections.title: Political Activities
sections.summary: Nishio's political-funds charge and 209 to 178 nonconfidence vote, a 30.1 billion yen budget revision, the National Property Law, Democratic Party defections, the 28 June Fukui earthquake (3,195 dead) and 1,136 internees at Sugamo.

sections.title: Economic Activities
sections.summary: May and April data: tenants bought 101,498 cho of land, coal output rose to 2,788,500 tons, coke hit a postwar peak, union membership reached 6.55 million, and the four-month trade deficit was 200 million dollars.

sections.title: Social Activities
sections.summary: First model health center at Morioka, new Pharmaceutical, Narcotics and Marihuana laws, 59,196 repatriates, the 18 June resolution nullifying the Imperial Rescript on Education, 124.9 million textbooks and Cardinal Spellman's visit.

sections.title: Part II: Political
sections.summary: Politics and law: the Nishio scandal, budget compromise of 30 June, illegal-transactions probes, the National Property Law, Fukui earthquake relief, judges' pay laws and war crimes totals (673 tried by 20 June).

sections.title: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Nishio scandal, the budget deadlock ended 30 June, illegal-transactions probes, the National Property Law, local finance bills, Diet business and party splits among Democrats and others.

sections.title: Political Developments
sections.summary: The antiadministration alliance resolved to overthrow the Ashida cabinet; government parties united at month's end to reject the nonconfidence vote against Nishio and moved toward budget agreement.

sections.title: Nishio Controversy
sections.summary: Nishio failed to report 500,000 yen in political funds, splitting the Social Democrats. The 24 June nonconfidence motion lost 209 to 178; Attorney General Suzuki said Nishio would resign after the budget passed, then be prosecuted.

sections.title: Budget Controversy
sections.summary: Budget deadlock ended in a 30 June compromise: fares set at 255 percent rather than a proposed 330 percent, a 30.1 billion yen change to the 399 billion yen General Account, and a 3,791 yen wage base.

sections.title: Zaibatsu Dissolution and Foreign Capital
sections.summary: Ashida told the Diet on 22 June that Zaibatsu dissolution was virtually complete. Official Horigoshi said little private foreign capital could be expected soon, citing taxes, labor unrest and undetermined exchange rates.

sections.title: Illegal Transactions
sections.summary: Procurators uncovered hoarded military goods (Nakajima, Tohoku Metals, Fuji Sanpro). The Diet committee probed Nishio's 500,000 yen, Democratic Party funds, the Gunma coffee case (governor resigned), Finance Minister Kitamura and Ono's perjury case.

sections.title: Government Activities
sections.summary: The National Property Law, passed 28 June, creates five classes of public property and a classification commission. Three local finance measures seek 199.4 billion yen; 34 prefectural conferences were held.

sections.title: The Diet
sections.summary: Diet bills introduced 26 May-25 June are tabulated; the political contributions bill was enacted 19 June. Both houses reaffirmed the 1890 Rescript on Education invalid (18-19 June); Takahashi and Fujieda won by-elections.

sections.title: Political Parties
sections.summary: Eight Democratic Diet members announced secession on 6 June over war bond interest deferment. Social Democrats approved nationalizing electric power; the People's Cooperative Party offered ten budget revisions; Democratic Liberals campaigned against Ashida.

sections.title: Public Safety
sections.summary: The 28 June Fukui earthquake destroyed about 70 percent of Fukui city and killed 3,195 there. A blast at the Mitsubishi-Katsuda mine killed 62; April offenses numbered 196,951 and prisoners 92,607.

sections.title: Legal Affairs and War Crimes
sections.summary: The Diet passed the administrative litigation law and judges' pay increases on 25 June. Sugamo held 1,136 internees; 673 suspects tried by 20 June, 623 convicted, 95 sentenced to death.

sections.title: Part III: Economic
sections.summary: Economic reports: May land sales of 101,498 cho, postwar peaks in coke and watches, coal output, textiles, power, the Broadcast Bill, union membership of 6.55 million, trade credits, finance and science.

sections.title: Agriculture and Fisheries
sections.summary: Tenants bought 101,498 cho in May (632,632 cho cumulative); reclamation lands 567,873 cho; cooperatives, crop insurance, April slaughter of 4,064 tons, fisheries and whaling.

sections.title: Agrarian Reform
sections.summary: Tenant farmers bought 101,498 cho in May, bringing agrarian-reform sales to 632,632 cho. Reclamation holdings reached 567,873 cho; 200,383 cho had passed to the Agriculture Ministry; 2,767 cho of demonstration farms were to be sold.

sections.title: Arable Land by Prefectures
sections.summary: Arable land was 12.49 percent of Japan Proper's 36,048,047 hectares at 31 August 1947; Hokkaido 9.40 percent. The farm population of 36,509,458 averaged 7.345 persons per hectare. Pages 46-49 are charts only.

sections.title: Livestock, Fisheries and Whaling
sections.summary: 5,470 cooperatives elected 75,473 directors and auditors; April slaughter fell to 4,064 tons; marine output nearly doubled to 222,509 tons. Antarctic whaling was authorized 21 June and 104 whales were taken.

sections.title: Forestry and Mining
sections.summary: May log output was 60,355,400 cubic feet and forests were overcut. Coal output reached 2,788,500 tons, below quota; crude oil 15,399 kiloliters; 13 of 33 minerals rose in April.

sections.title: Heavy Industries
sections.summary: Coke reached a postwar peak of 254,819 tons in May and ammonium sulfate 104,765 tons. Rolled steel rose 5.6 percent, cement fell to 141,883 tons, and shipyards completed 21 steel vessels.

sections.title: Manufacturing
sections.summary: Wheat flour fell sharply in April amid depleted grain stocks; beer rose 20 percent. Small trucks hit a postwar peak of 243, typewriters rose 361 percent, and watches and clocks reached 197,039.

sections.title: Textile Industries
sections.summary: The Fukui earthquake threatened rayon rehabilitation. Raw silk output was 10,536 bales; cotton yarn was held down while fabrics rose; rayon, wool, bast fibers, garments and dyeing are reported.

sections.title: Cotton
sections.summary: May raw cotton imports dropped 3,347,000 pounds; pure yarn output held at 23.9 million pounds. Independent weavers gained 4,678,000 square yards of fabric, and operating looms reached 105,277.

sections.title: Silk
sections.summary: Raw silk output was 10,536 bales in May and 11,856 bales were tested for export. The spring cocoon crop was estimated at 77,379,000 pounds; silk fabric hit a postwar record of 10,631,000 square yards.

sections.title: Artificial Fibers
sections.summary: Rayon staple and filament output set postwar records, up 589,000 and 380,000 pounds. Imports included 1,700 tons of rayon pulp and the first nylon waste; Kurashiki began commercial polyvinyl alcohol fiber.

sections.title: Wool
sections.summary: May wool imports totaled 3,183 bales, but little of the 9,605 bales received since 1 April reached mills because of inspection and distribution delays. Woolen fabric reached 1,571,000 square yards.

sections.title: Hard and Bast Fibers, Garments and Finishing
sections.summary: The seventh postwar abaca shipment, 6,558 bales, arrived. Flax yarn rose 10 percent, but ramie, hemp and jute fell after a strike at the largest ramie and hemp mill; cotton printing set a postwar record.

sections.title: Transportation and Public Utilities
sections.summary: Registered motor vehicles numbered 209,002 in May; railways carried 565,601,143 passengers. Coastal cargo rose 11.4 percent to 1,129,958 tons, and power generation was 2,974,000,000 kWh.

sections.title: Communications
sections.summary: The Cabinet approved a Broadcast Bill on 18 June creating a Broadcasting Commission and a nonprofit Broadcasting Corporation. Telephones reached 1,322,017, radio licensees 6,650,046, and 988,505 vacuum tubes were produced.

sections.title: Labor
sections.summary: Left-right struggle in unions, the Labor-Farmer Liaison Council, 31,075 unions with 6.55 million members, labor relations disputes, a 3,700 yen wage base, employment and labor education.

sections.title: Labor and Employer Organizations
sections.summary: The Labor-Farmer Liaison Council (9 June) and Tokyo Council of Independent Labor Unions (12 June, 125,000 members) were founded. Unions numbered 31,075 with 6,553,816 members; SCAP did not object to ILO observers.

sections.title: Labor Relations
sections.summary: Coal unions ratified grievance machinery; Tokyo-Yokohama rail locals struck for 24 hours. The CLRC set a ¥3,923 private railway base wage and settled the All-Japan Express dispute at ¥4,854; Toho Studio cut 1,019 jobs.

sections.title: Wages, Working Conditions and Employment
sections.summary: Wage stabilization set ¥3,700 as the base for 23 June price revisions; government workers sought ¥5,200. April manufacturing wages rose 14 percent; inspections numbered 9,955 with 19,019 violations.

sections.title: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Boeki Cho was authorized 28 May to deal directly with foreign firms. A $60 million U.S. cotton credit, a 31 May sterling agreement and a 9 June China trade agreement followed; the four-month deficit reached $200,186,092.

sections.title: Price and Distribution
sections.summary: Full ration needs were met, with imported sugar substituted for five days. The Cabinet approved fish and vegetable control plans 1 June; milk, vegetable and grain prices rose, and 12,500 ration "ghosts" were caught.

sections.title: Finance
sections.summary: Nine foreign banks' licenses were broadened 14 June. Bank of Japan notes stood at 230.6 billion yen, tax collections reached 147.2 billion yen (108.7 percent of estimate), and national debt totaled 365.6 billion yen.

sections.title: Property Control and Reparations
sections.summary: Looted property custody centered on 39.5 million yen of cinchona bark; 246 vessels were deleted from looted lists. The SCAP Custody Account reached 284,957,133 yen; 14,122 machine tools had shipped to claimants by 30 June.

sections.title: Science and Technology
sections.summary: The Cabinet approved the Science Council Bill 8 June. Professor Honda discovered a new comet 3 June; 1,327 Japanese Standards were in effect and patent registrations totaled 123.

sections.title: Part IV: Social
sections.summary: Social reports: communicable diseases, new pharmaceutical and narcotics laws, public assistance, repatriation, the Rescript on Education invalidation, religion, public opinion surveys, press, radio, film and libraries.

sections.title: Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Communicable diseases rose to 4,399 cases in May; the Pharmaceutical Affairs Law passed 30 June and narcotics laws 28 June. May public assistance reached 1,911,666 persons; repatriates numbered about 59,000.

sections.title: Preventive Medicine and Veterinary Affairs
sections.summary: A model health center opened at Morioka 15 June. Eleven principal communicable diseases caused 4,399 cases and 430 deaths in May; the Councillors passed the Preventive Vaccination and Venereal Disease Prevention Laws.

sections.title: Medical Administration and Supply
sections.summary: The Pharmaceutical Affairs Law passed 30 June, requiring accredited pharmacists. Japan had 3,451 hospitals with 310,562 beds; May medical supply output was 1.94 billion yen; narcotics laws passed 28 June, with 82,324 handlers registered.

sections.title: Public Assistance, Vital Statistics and Repatriation
sections.summary: May public assistance reached 1,911,666 persons, with payments of 377 million yen. April births were 324,393 and deaths 79,756; 59,198 persons were repatriated, mostly from Soviet areas.

sections.title: Education, Religion, Cultural Resources and Media of Expression
sections.summary: The Rescript on Education invalidated, a 1948 education budget of 26.7 billion yen, boards of education, textbooks, Cardinal Spellman's visit, opinion surveys, press, radio, film, music and libraries.

sections.title: Education
sections.summary: The Councillors reaffirmed on 18 June the 1890 Imperial Rescript on Education is invalid. The education budget carried 5,381,320,000 yen for school buildings; 687 textbook manuscripts were announced and 1,850 characters standardized.

sections.title: Religion and Cultural Resources
sections.summary: Cardinal Spellman and 14 Catholic officials visited Tokyo 7 June; 46 religious workers were cleared to enter. Applications for transfer of state precincts (72,000 shrines, 30,000 temples) closed.

sections.title: Media of Expression
sections.summary: A 19-newspaper Public Opinion League formed; 821 new book editions appeared in May and 98 foreign books were licensed. The first press-code prosecution (Nikkan Sports) occurred; new SCAP libraries opened at Kanazawa and Kobe.

sections.title: Map of Japan - Topography
sections.summary: Final page: a topographic map of Japan, with the back cover and a printing-plant mark.
